query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with an fcc matrix, degradation during elevated-temperature exposure is primarily governed by the selective oxidation of the most reactive elements (especially Ti and Al) at the alloy surface and grain boundaries. This oxidation leads to a non-protective, porous oxide scale and local elemental depletion that induce stress concentrations and microcrack formation; these processes ultimately trigger catastrophic failure in oxidizing atmospheres.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy exhibiting a homogeneous fcc matrix.
generation.intervention: Switch the test gas environment from a controlled oxidizing mixture (with a specified oxygen partial pressure) to a reducing mixture (with a specified hydrogen partial pressure) while maintaining the same elevated-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Both sets of samples are exposed under identical thermal cycles and temperatures characteristic of service conditions. The oxidizing condition uses a controlled oxygen-containing inert mixture, while the reducing condition employs a gas mixture with a controlled, low oxygen (or added hydrogen) content. All other variables (time, heating/cooling rates) remain constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation and evolution of a porous, non-protective oxide scale, with localized depletion of Ti and Al at grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing environment, the preferential oxidation of Ti and Al creates a discontinuous oxide scale and depletion zones, which serve as stress concentrators that promote microcrack nucleation and propagation, ultimately leading to catastrophic failure. In a reducing environment, the suppressed formation of these oxides should alleviate the local chemical and mechanical imbalances, thereby reducing the rate of degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline oxidizing condition that exhibits significant oxide scale formation, local elemental depletion, and crack-induced failure, samples under reducing conditions should show reduced oxide scale formation, minimal elemental depletion at grain boundaries, and fewer microcracks, resulting in improved mechanical integrity during high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The initial observed degradation behavior under oxidizing conditions in as-built, additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to elevated-temperature exposures under controlled gas compositions where the oxidizing versus reducing nature of the environment (defined by oxygen or hydrogen partial pressures) is the key variable.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact oxidation kinetics, the thickness and morphology of the oxide scale, and the precise quantitative thresholds for elemental depletion that lead to critical crack formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identically fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA samples. Expose one set to an oxidizing gas environment (fixed oxygen partial pressure) and the other to a reducing environment (controlled low oxygen or controlled hydrogen partial pressure) at the same elevated temperature and time duration. Post-exposure, undertake microstructural and mechanical analysis.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and continuity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Local elemental composition at grain boundaries using energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS)
Mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness or tensile tests) to assess structural integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples in the reducing environment display oxide scale characteristics, elemental depletion, microcrack densities, and mechanical property degradation similar to those in the oxidizing environment, or if catastrophic failure occurs regardless of the gas composition, then the hypothesis that oxidation-driven elemental depletion is the governing mechanism is falsified.
